title: How to fix the US air traffic system? So far, billions in spending have fallen short.
text:
How to fix the US air traffic system? So far, billions in spending have fallen short.
Massive amounts of money have been spent on upgrades to the U.S. air traffic control system, but after a nationwide ground stop, the FAA is asking for even more.
The technical outage that grounded 3,500 domestic flights, canceled about 12,500 more, and stranded 1.5 million passengers across the United States on Friday has landed in Congress, with Trump administration officials meeting some pushback on their plans to make sure such an event never happens again.
At a weekly policy lunch for Republican senators, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy lobbied for his $50 billion spending plan to maintain and replace the nation’s decades-old air traffic control system, which is at the heart of the breakdown.
“The longer we stay on an old rickety network, the less safe it becomes,” Mr. Duffy told reporters after his meeting. “I’m making a nice ask, and I’m going to let them go through the process,” he added, as he asked for bipartisan support.
Successive presidential administrations have funneled billions of dollars to the Federal Aviation Administration, so it can upgrade old technology and make other improvements to U.S. air traffic control, airports, and other aspects of air travel. But a recent system failure has renewed a debate over funding.
But that support is not coming easily. Many Democrats say the administration hasn’t spent all of the $12.5 billion Congress already allocated for upgrades. House Appropriations Committee Ranking Member Rosa DeLauro called the new request “ransom without a real plan to deliver.” Even some Republicans say they will not sign on to more funding without receiving more details about how it will be spent.
For Republican Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana, Secretary Duffy’s request sounds much too expensive and vague.
“We’re not going to give them $50 billion, but I think that we are willing to provide the money to replace the copper wires with the fiber optic and to try to stop the bleeding,” Senator Kennedy told reporters Tuesday.
The FAA outage is part of a series of technical failures demonstrating that many of America’s systems for safety, communications, and business are aging and vulnerable. In the past week, a number of older legacy technical systems failed: Microsoft Outlook shut down Thursday, halting email traffic for millions of Americans. Chase electronic and ATM banking systems shut down on Monday. And on Tuesday, the top-secret internal communications of America’s largest intelligence agency, the National Security Agency, went down.
In a House Homeland Security Committee hearing Wednesday, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said that the various outages appear not to be acts of sabotage. Jay Clayton, Director of National Intelligence, said they were “separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes.”
Virginia Sen. Mark Warner told reporters Wednesday that “companies are rushing at an unprecedented level” to patch system flaws discovered by artificial intelligence.
“We’re going to have more of this,” he said. “We should warn the public.”
Upgrades aren’t keeping pace
The FAA outage was not unanticipated. The Biden administration passed an infrastructure bill in 2021 that included $25 billion in upgrades to aging airports and air traffic control systems. Even with the spending, the Government Accountability Office issued a 2024 report finding that 51 of the FAA’s 138 air traffic information systems were “unsustainable,” with outdated functionality and a lack of spare parts. The report concluded that the FAA “has been slow to modernize the most critical and at-risk systems.”
Earlier this year, Secretary Duffy told Congress he would need an additional $30 billion to upgrade the system; after the ground stop, his request rose to $50 billion. The rising funding target rankled Democrats and Republicans. Democrats say the administration has spent only $5 billion of $14.4 billion it authorized for air traffic system upgrades.
The Trump administration’s greatest challenge will be pushing through a massive appropriations package at a time when a Republican-led Congress has only a few weeks left on its schedule.
Democratic leaders, who will take control of both the House and Senate in January 2027, issued a letter demanding answers about the Nov. 13 outage. “Congress deserves clear answers on how the FAA is ensuring the safety of the aviation system for the traveling public while these new systems are being deployed,” wrote the Democratic senators on the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, led by ranking members Maria Cantwell and Tammy Duckworth.
Senate Republican Majority Leader John Thune blames Democrats for blocking additional funding in the final weeks of Congress.
“Democrats are not engaging in a conversation at all when it comes to funding government, and that’s a problem,” he told reporters after the meeting with Secretary Duffy. Democrats have blocked 12 appropriations bills on everything from defense authorization and the farm bill to air traffic safety, Senator Thune said.
Work on the system is ongoing
R. John Hansman, an MIT aeronautics professor, says that America’s system has been underfunded for decades, but despite that, “it operates really well.” Replacing this network will be extremely complex, a bit like renovating a house while living in it. “You can replace everything using the technology that you already have, or you can take advantage of the new technologies we are seeing today.”
The good news about last week’s ground stop, he says, is that “nobody hesitated to shut down the system” when there were signs that something was interfering with the communications between air traffic controllers and pilots.
“We have an obligation to not do anything that compromises the safety of the existing system,” he says. But as the upgrade project proceeds, “we will have other unanticipated issues like this one because of the complications of the existing system. We need to have a plan for how to do this.”
While the cause for Friday’s shutdown is still not fully understood, investigators agree that the incident was triggered when a technician for L3Harris Technologies was replacing a router in El Dorado, Arkansas. The old system used copper-wire networks, and the replacement will introduce new fiber-optic cable systems, which would expand that volume of information flowing between air traffic controllers and pilots. Unfortunately, the new router proved faulty and disrupted communications and radar systems across the country.
FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford told reporters that the new router had been tested for a year, and that 68 previous router installations by L3Harris had occurred without incident. The FAA has paused this portion of the upgrade until they understand why the fault occurred. The Washington Post reported that an FAA official supervised and signed off on the work in El Dorado that led to the outage.
But Transportation Department officials note that the upgrade continues. The Biden administration replaced 19% of the existing copper-wire networks with fiber optic, and the Trump administration has updated 50% of the system in one year.
In addition, Duffy’s department has used some of the $12.5 billion it has received to deploy new technology at 143 control towers, convert 469 radio sites to modernized systems, and to install other new tech such as electronic flight strips, tower simulation systems, and surface movement radars.
In the House hearing on Wednesday, Democratic Rep. LaMonica McIver rejected Republican claims that Congress has failed to fund aviation system repairs. She noted the Biden administration funding, and that Mr. Mullin as a Republican congressman had voted against it.
Other Democrats have offered tentative support. Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen told CNN he would support the money necessary to fix the U.S. air traffic control system. But he added, “Congress has given the administration what they ask for.”
“If they need more, they should come up and justify it,” Senator Van Hollen said.
Caitlin Babcock and Victoria Hoffmann contributed reporting from Washington, and Zachery Proctor contributed from Boston.
